text:
Temu and Italy's ICQRF Partner to Strengthen Protection of Geographical Indications Online
New Memorandum of Understanding establishes a cooperation framework focused on prevention, seller guidance, information exchange and the protection of Geographical Indications on Temu
ROME, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Temu and Italy's Central Inspectorate for Fraud Repression and Quality Protection of Agri-Food Products (ICQRF) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen the protection of Geographical Indications (GIs) on Temu's marketplace.
The agreement, signed in conjunction with an event marking ICQRF's 40th anniversary, places a strong emphasis on prevention. Temu and ICQRF will cooperate to provide sellers with appropriate information and guidance and will meet periodically to evaluate and develop joint initiatives aimed at strengthening the protection of GIs and preventing unfair commercial practices.
ICQRF is part of Italy's Ministry of Agriculture, Food Sovereignty and Forests (MASAF) and is the competent authority responsible for official controls on agri-food and wine products, with specific responsibilities relating to GIs. It is also part of the European network of competent national and EU authorities involved in GI protection and cooperates with stakeholders on agri-food and wine verification.
"Geographical Indications are an important part of Italy's renowned agri-food heritage, and protecting them in the digital environment requires close cooperation across the ecosystem," said a Temu spokesperson. "This agreement with ICQRF allows us to combine prevention, information and guidance for sellers, and ongoing information exchange with effective mechanisms for addressing potential infringements. By working together, we can promote best practices across our marketplace and strengthen the protection of Geographical Indications online."
The agreement also establishes an ongoing framework for cooperation and information exchange between Temu and ICQRF, with dedicated points of contact to facilitate regulatory clarification, address practical issues and coordinate the monitoring and development of activities under the MoU.
"The agreement with Temu represents another key milestone in ICQRF's strategy to protect Geographical Indications in international digital markets. Structured cooperation with leading online marketplaces is essential to combat online infringements and make the protection of our quality products increasingly effective," said Dr. Felice Assenza, Head of Department at ICQRF.
"In Temu, we have found a partner that is attentive and responsive to the need for effective protection and that, from the outset, has demonstrated a genuine willingness to engage in dialogue and cooperation. We are confident that this agreement will further strengthen the protection of the authenticity and reputation of Italian excellence," Dr. Assenza said.
Temu has introduced a dedicated GI category within its global Brand Registry, strengthening the tools available to GI rights holders worldwide. Rights holders and authorised agents can register their GI rights by submitting the relevant registration details and supporting documentation for Temu's review. Once approved, they can report potentially infringing listings directly through Temu's Brand Protection Center, providing a clearer and more streamlined route for GI-related complaints.
For Temu, the agreement builds on its ongoing work to advance intellectual property protection and promote best practices across its marketplace. Intellectual property protection is a core pillar of Temu's platform governance, supported by comprehensive policies and measures designed to protect rights holders.
About Temu
Temu is a global e-commerce platform connecting consumers with millions of manufacturers, brands and business partners. Operating in more than 90 markets worldwide, Temu is committed to providing affordable, high-quality products that enable customers to live better lives.
About ICQRF
The Central Inspectorate for Fraud Repression and Quality Protection of Agri-Food Products (ICQRF) is part of Italy's Ministry of Agriculture, Food Sovereignty and Forests (MASAF). ICQRF is the Italian competent authority responsible for official controls on agri-food and wine products, with specific responsibilities relating to Geographical Indications. It also designates and supervises public and private entities responsible for controls and certification activities relating to Geographical Indications.

title: Temu Introduces New GI Protection Feature to Support Local Producers
description: DUBLIN, Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Temu has added a new dedicated geographical indications (GI) category to its Brand Registry Portal to support local producers and strengthen the safeguarding of authentic GI products online. Available across all markets, t…
text:
Temu Introduces New GI Protection Feature to Support Local Producers
DUBLIN, Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Temu has added a new dedicated geographical indications (GI) category to its Brand Registry Portal to support local producers and strengthen the safeguarding of authentic GI products online. Available across all markets, the new GI feature gives rightsholders a direct way to cooperate with Temu and submit notifications concerning potential GI infringements for review.
Geographical indications identify products whose qualities or reputation are linked to their geographical origin, carrying economic, social and cultural value for local communities. Protecting these rights online helps maintain consumer trust and supports producers whose livelihoods depend on the reputation of their products. The dedicated GI category builds on Temu's existing support for IP protection by making the process more streamlined and accessible.
The GI feature is among the latest measures that Temu has introduced to support businesses, drawing from feedback from more than 100 meetings with trade associations, chambers of commerce and start-up networks across Europe, where complexity emerged as a recurring barrier to doing online business.
"We want to support local businesses with practical tools that reduce complexity," said a Temu spokesperson. "For GI rightsholders, this means a clearer way to work directly with us to help protect the authenticity of their products and the expertise and heritage behind them."
The update is part of Temu's broader IP protection efforts, which combine cooperation with rightsholders, proactive monitoring, proprietary technology and human expert review.
According to Temu's 2026 Intellectual Property Protection Report, the company's proactive monitoring database covers more than 15,000 brands. Proactive removals of potentially infringing listings outnumbered reactive takedowns by 331 to 1 during the reporting period. Temu also works directly with more than 3,000 brands through its Brand Guardian Initiative and provides IP compliance resources through its Seller Education Center.

Digest: McDonald’s Bets on $1bn Ad Business; Temu Cuts Fake Influencer Network on Meta
by on 28th Sep 2026 in News
In today’s Digest, we discuss McDonald’s betting on a USD$1bn (£750m) ad business as it joins the commerce-media gold rush, Temu cutting a USD$1bn (£750m) fake influencer network on Meta, and TikTok settling with Alabama for USD$100m (£75m) over teen use.
McDonald’s bets on $1bn ad business
McDonald's has revealed a new venture, McDonald's Media Network, with ambitions to become a USD$1bn (£750m) advertising operation. The fast-food giants plans to turn its digital presence and physical consumer touchpoints into a home for advertising...
The company does not merely want to sell burgers, but own a sequence of touchpoints: the app, the kiosk, the loyalty programme, the physical restaurant each generating attention, identity and purchase data.
Temu cuts $1bn fake influencer network on Meta
Temu has quietly dismantled a nearly USD$1bn (£750m) network of suspected fake influencer accounts on Meta's platforms. The company had been funding partnership ads through influencers and creators on Instagram and Facebook, targeting audiences across the UK and all 27 EU countries. This is according to Online Risk Labs, a Czech research group that examined 16 months of Temu's advertising activity through April 2026.
Of the 100 accounts featuring the most Temu ads, ORL found roughly 73 were likely fake, many carrying nonsensical names, based in China, Russia, Bangladesh or Iran, and frequently changing identities. Together, those 100 accounts ran more than 1.4 million partnership ads, reaching a combined audience of nearly 17 billion views. Within days, 90 of the flagged accounts stopped running Temu ads entirely, and total partnership ad volume from the company nearly halved.
Neither Temu nor Meta responded to requests for comment.
TikTok settles with Alabama for $100m over teen use
TikTok has settled its first-ever state lawsuit over teen safety, agreeing to pay Alabama at least USD$100m (£75m) and overhaul how the app works for younger users. Alabama's attorney general, Steve Marshall, accused the platform of designing itself to be addictive and harming teenagers' mental health. Under the settlement, teens aged 13 to 17 will face a default two-hour daily time limit, automatic lockouts between midnight and 6 am, and "productive pauses" interrupting continuous use at 15, 60 and 90 minutes.
TikTok admitted no wrongdoing and continues to deny Alabama's claims, but Marshall called it a milestone for parents, saying the company has finally agreed to give them real control over what their kids see and how long they spend on the app.#

title: Temu axed its $1 billion network of fake influencer accounts on Meta
description: Temu had spent nearly $1 billion funding partnership ads with various influencers and creators, many of which appeared to be fake accounts.
text:
Temu appears to have largely stopped funding a network of fake accounts on Meta’s platforms in the days after it was first exposed by Fortune.
Temu had spent nearly $1 billion funding partnership ads with various influencers and creators on Instagram and Facebook, targeting users in the U.K. and all 27 EU countries, according to Online Risk Labs, a Czech-based social media research group. ORL examined a sample period of Temu’s advertising activity over 16 months ending in April 2026.
Around 73 of the 100 influencers whose pages featured the most Temu ads were probably fake, according to ORL. The accounts often had nonsensical names, were based in China, Russia, Bangladesh, or Iran, and some of them frequently changed names—all symptoms of inauthentic activity, according to ORL.
These 100 accounts participated in more than 1.4 million partnership ads, achieving a cumulative reach of almost 17 billion pairs of eyeballs, ORL told Fortune. (Meta’s partnership ad program allows influencers to create content that promotes a brand, tagging the company in each post. If the company likes the content, it can pay to boost it just like a paid ad. Creators get a cut of the budget. Meta disclosed earlier this year that partnership ads were on course for a $10 billion annual run rate across Facebook and Instagram.)
Fortune’s story on the fake account network ran on Aug. 31. At that time, Temu was running 4,900 separate partnership campaigns a day on the network.
By Sept. 4, 90 accounts suddenly featured zero advertising from Temu. Of the top 100 accounts, 54 stopped using partnership ads almost immediately after Aug. 31. (Temu’s entire network of creators involves 12,000 or more accounts, many of which are legit.) Overall, the number of partnership ads run by Temu almost halved after Fortune’s story.
The biggest account, “Ya Lili,” had 183,000 followers on her @findgadgetswithme Instagram account and a further 129,000 followers on Facebook, where she went by the name “Must good.” Ya Lili’s content ran in 278,000 Temu ad campaigns in ORL’s study period—about 225 campaigns per day.
Her account is almost certainly a fake. By Sept. 4, only five ads from Ya Lili appeared on Meta’s platforms, probably as remnants from previously scheduled ad buys. Ya Lili previously posted multiple times per day, but she stopped posting entirely on Sept. 7.
Neither Temu nor Meta responded to messages requesting comment.
“When you look at their Instagram accounts, you can see that they have not published any new posts/reels since two weeks or so. These are predominantly the accounts based in Russia, with some also based in the United States or China,” ORL manager Vendula Prokůpková told Fortune. “We also noticed that most of the Instagram accounts of these ‘creators’ no longer display information about the country the account is based in.”
Temu’s ad budget appears to have been maintained for legitimate creators. “Across all of its pages, weekly ads went from 166,523 in the week of 17 August to 147,013 in the week of 7 September,” ORL said in a follow-up to its original study. “Partnership ads over the same weeks went from 115,114 to 64,008.”
Partnership ads in Ireland, Cyprus, Austria, Denmark, Latvia, and Slovenia ceased almost entirely, ORL said. It is not clear why. The laws against misleading advertising in those jurisdictions are very strict, however. In Ireland, Denmark, Cyprus, and Austria, penalties can include criminal conviction and imprisonment. In the others, consumers have the right to sue companies that publish misleading ads, and cases can result in companies being forced to pay a percentage of their revenues.

title: TEMU PARTNERS WITH CITEA TO SUPPORT CYPRUS' DIGITAL BUSINESS COMMUNITY
description: NICOSIA, Cyprus, Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Temu has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Cyprus Information Technology Enterprises Association (CITEA) to support Cyprus' technology and business community with new digital growth opportuniti…
text:
Temu Partners with CITEA to Support Cyprus' Digital Business Community
NICOSIA, Cyprus, Sept. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Temu has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Cyprus Information Technology Enterprises Association (CITEA) to support Cyprus' technology and business community with new digital growth opportunities.
Through the partnership, Temu will collaborate with CITEA's programmes, events, and network of member companies, contributing to initiatives that promote digital entrepreneurship and business development. CITEA, as the representative body of Cyprus' Information and Communications Technology sector, will support engagement between its members and Temu, highlighting opportunities for Cypriot companies to leverage digital platforms, explore new markets, and strengthen their global competitiveness.
The partnership builds on Temu's existing presence in Cyprus, where it introduced its Local Seller Program in 2025, providing eligible local businesses with access to digital commerce opportunities and the potential to expand their reach to customers across Europe.
For CITEA, the collaboration reflects its ongoing commitment to supporting the growth and internationalisation of Cyprus' technology ecosystem by connecting its members with global platforms, encouraging innovation, and creating pathways for local businesses to compete in an increasingly digital global economy.
"Partnering with a global leader in e-commerce like Temu creates meaningful opportunities for our members and the wider ICT business community," said George Malekkos, President of CITEA. "At CITEA, we are committed to helping Cypriot technology companies expand their reach, embrace new digital opportunities, and compete internationally. This collaboration gives our members greater visibility and access to European markets, while reinforcing Cyprus' position as an innovative and outward-looking technology hub."
Alongside CITEA, Temu will participate in local initiatives to connect directly with Cypriot entrepreneurs and companies within the digital business community. The partnership aims to foster collaboration, support local entrepreneurship, and highlight success stories demonstrating how Cypriot businesses can use digital tools and platforms to grow internationally. Both organisations will work together on shared communications to showcase opportunities for local merchants and businesses.
"Cyprus is home to an ambitious entrepreneurial community," said a Temu spokesperson. "Our collaboration with CITEA gives us a direct line to help local businesses embrace digital channels, tap into international demand, and thrive across new markets."
END
About CITEA
The Cyprus Information Technology Enterprises Association (CITEA) was founded in 1987 and is the principal representative body for ICT enterprises in Cyprus, with more than 100 member companies spanning software, cloud infrastructure, systems integration, and related fields. CITEA is an active member of the World Information Technology and Services Alliance (WITSA), DigitalEurope, and the Cyprus Employers and Industrialists Federation (OEB). More information is available at citea.cy.
About Temu
Temu is a global e-commerce platform connecting consumers with millions of manufacturers, brands and business partners. Operating in more than 90 markets worldwide, Temu is committed to providing affordable, high-quality products that enable customers to live better lives.

title: China's Temu may have spent as much as $962 millionon Meta ads in the UK and Europe, with 73 of its top 100 creators likely fake
description: Temu may have spent nearly one billion dollars on Meta ads promoting products.  Research suggests many boosted accounts likely do not represent real influencers.  These accounts, often based in Russia and China, promoted Temu products extensively.  This pract…
text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Of the 100 creators whose content was most heavily boosted by Temu across the UK and Europe, 73 were likely fake accounts, according to research by Online Risk Labs (ORL). Only eight of the top 100 creators were verified as real identities, while 28 were based in Russia and 19 in China. Just six were based in the EU or UK.
One of the accounts identified in the research belongs to Ya Lili, who has about 183,000 followers on Instagram under the handle “@findgadgetswithme”. The account posts videos promoting Temu products, including a recent video featuring a shower scrubber, with a link directing viewers to Temu.
According to ORL, Ya Lili was Temu’s top creator for partnership ads on Meta platforms in the UK and Europe. The research suggests the account almost certainly does not represent a real person.
Real money going to fake accounts
Ya Lili also has about 129,000 followers on Facebook, where the account uses the name “Must good”. Its listed location is “England, Birmingham, MO, United States”, while its bio says “You are my dream of dead”. The account’s email address also appears to be Chinese.
ORL said Temu-boosted posts from the account were viewed more than 1 billion times across Facebook and Instagram during the 16 months ending in April 2026. The content appeared in nearly 109,541 Temu ad campaigns, equivalent to about 225 campaigns a day.
ORL estimates that Temu spent as much as $962 million on similar ads across the UK and 27 EU countries during the period. The estimate is based on total impressions and average cost per reach. The research group estimates that Temu accounts for nearly 2% of Meta’s revenue from the continent in any given quarter.
“Among the top 100 influencers collaborating with Temu, there are certainly some real people among them. In my estimate, however, they account for no more than 15–20%. By contrast, I have serious doubts about the authenticity of accounts that, according to the platform, are based in Russia, China, or Iran,” ORL manager Vendula Prokůpková told Fortune.
Legal questions for Temu
The findings could also raise regulatory questions, as European advertising rules prohibit misleading commercial practices. Stuart Lester, who leads the advertising and marketing group at London law firm Mishcon de Reya, said accounts presented as real individuals when they are not could potentially breach those rules.
“By all means utilise Facebook and Instagram and influencers, but know that there are rules that you have to abide by, and you certainly can’t be creating fake accounts and portraying these as real individuals. That’s misleading on many levels,” Reya explained.
It remains unclear whether Temu knowingly works with such accounts or is itself being deceived by scammers. There is also no evidence that the products or advertisements promoted through the accounts are themselves fraudulent.
ORL has filed a report with the EU’s Digital Services Act regulator, asking it to assess the risks associated with Temu’s influencer accounts.
The findings also highlight the growing challenge posed by AI-generated content, automated account creation and performance-optimisation systems in digital advertising, as such tools become more prevalent across the industry.
